learn.title: How it works
learn.intro: Every picture in Mirrorfold is made by arithmetic. There are no drawings in it and no stored shapes. These lessons build one of the most famous pictures in mathematics from nothing but multiplying and adding. Each step has something to drag, and none of it needs more than school arithmetic.
learn.track.mandel: From one number to the Mandelbrot set

learn.figure: Drawing for this step. Drag in it, or use the arrow keys.
learn.mandel.square.title: Multiply a number by itself, again and again
learn.mandel.square.text: Pick a number and multiply it by itself. That is called squaring it. Now take the answer and square that. Keep going. Only three things can happen. A number smaller than one gets smaller every time, and creeps toward zero. A number bigger than one gets bigger every time, faster and faster, and runs away. And one itself never moves, because one times one is one. A number below zero turns positive on the first step, because a minus times a minus is a plus.
learn.mandel.square.do: Drag the dot along the line. Find the exact place where shrinking turns into running away.
learn.mandel.square.name: Doing the same thing over and over, feeding each answer back in, is called iteration. The list of answers is called a sequence. Zero and one are called fixed points, because the rule leaves them where they are.
learn.mandel.addc.title: Add the same number after every squaring
learn.mandel.addc.text: Change the rule a little. Start from zero. Square it, then add a number that you choose. Call that number c. Then square the answer and add c again, and keep going. The question now is which values of c keep the answers close, and which send them running away. The answer is no longer simple. Some values of c settle on one number. Some bounce between two numbers for ever, or between three. Some wander with no pattern at all.
learn.mandel.addc.do: Slide c to minus 1, and watch the answers bounce between two places. Then try minus 1.755, where they visit three. Then find the largest c that does not run away.
learn.mandel.addc.name: A rule that turns each answer into the next one is called a recurrence, and the path the answers take is called an orbit. The bright bar under the line marks every c whose orbit stays close. It runs from minus 2 to one quarter. Remember that bar. It comes back in step five.
learn.mandel.plane.title: Numbers with two parts
learn.mandel.plane.text: A number on a line can only go left or right. So give it a second part, and let it be a point on a flat sheet. One part says how far across it is, and the other says how far up. To square such a point, do two things. Measure its distance from the middle, and square that distance. Measure its angle from the line that points right, and double that angle. That is all. Squaring a number on the line was this same rule all along: its angle was zero, and twice zero is zero.
learn.mandel.plane.do: Drag the blue dot. The pink dot is its square. Put the blue dot straight up, one unit from the middle, and see where its square lands.
learn.mandel.plane.name: These two-part numbers are called complex numbers. The part across is called the real part, and the part up is called the imaginary part. That is an unlucky name, because it is no more imaginary than a point on a map. The point one unit straight up is called i. Its angle is a quarter turn, so its square sits at a half turn, which is minus one. That is the whole meaning of the famous statement that i squared is minus one.
learn.mandel.hops.title: The same rule on the sheet
learn.mandel.hops.text: Now use the rule from step two with two-part numbers. Start at the middle. Square the point, add c, and repeat. This time c is a point as well, so adding it means sliding across and up by its two parts. Each hop is drawn as a line. The ring has a radius of two. Once a hop lands outside the ring, the point can never come back, and its distance grows without end. So the question for each c is simple. Does it ever leave the ring?
learn.mandel.hops.do: Drag c slowly around. Find a place where the hops spiral inward to one spot. Find one where they settle on a triangle. Then find the edge, where the smallest move changes everything.
learn.mandel.hops.name: This is the orbit from step two, now in the complex plane. The ring is called the escape radius. Places where the tiniest change at the start changes the whole outcome are what people mean by chaos.
learn.mandel.pixels.title: Ask the question for every square of a grid
learn.mandel.pixels.text: Here is how the picture is made. Lay a grid over the sheet. For each square, take the point at its middle as c, and count the hops until it leaves the ring. If it leaves quickly, paint the square a dark colour. If it takes longer, paint it brighter. If it has not left after two hundred hops, paint it black. Nobody draws the shape. It is only the same small question, asked once for every square.
learn.mandel.pixels.do: Make the grid finer and watch the shape appear. Tap any square to see its hops. Then look along the middle of the picture, from left to right. It is the bar from step two.
learn.mandel.pixels.name: The black shape is the Mandelbrot set: every c whose orbit never escapes. It is named after Benoit Mandelbrot, who studied it with a computer in 1980. A square of the grid is what a screen calls a pixel, and a picture made this way is called an escape-time picture.
learn.mandel.patience.title: How long to wait before giving up
learn.mandel.patience.text: The black shape is every c that never leaves the ring. But a computer cannot wait for never. It can only count up to some limit and then give up. Set the limit to one hop, and everything inside the ring counts as staying. Raise the limit, and each extra hop carves a little more away. The true shape is what remains when the limit grows without end. Every picture of it, however fine, is only the best guess so far.
learn.mandel.patience.do: Start with the limit at one, and raise it one hop at a time. Watch the ring turn into the shape.
learn.mandel.patience.name: A value that is approached as a count grows without end is called a limit, and it is the idea underneath calculus. The exact area of the Mandelbrot set is still not known. It is about one and a half, and nobody has found a formula for it.
learn.r.one: Stays close: it settles on one place.
learn.r.many: Stays close: it visits {0} places in turn.
learn.r.none: Stays close, with no simple pattern.
